venue_now: arXiv v2, 2 May 2026 (p. 1); no venue header in this text (the ethics section invokes the ACL Code of Ethics, p. 13); papers.json records Findings of ACL 2026, pp. 36308-36334
what_it_is: EngiBench is a hierarchical benchmark of engineering problem solving at three levels: foundational knowledge retrieval, contextual reasoning and open-ended modelling (pp. 1, 4). Levels 1 and 2 are closed-form problems taken from existing benchmarks (SuperGPQA, MMLU, MATH, GSM8k, Orca-Math, HARP, Omni-MATH, Big-Math), competition datasets and university course materials. They were filtered for engineering relevance by LLM prompts with human verification (pp. 5, 13-14). Level 3 holds 43 open-ended problems from modelling competitions with official rubrics (pp. 5, 14-15). An LLM rewrites each Level 1-2 problem into perturbed, knowledge-enhanced and math-abstraction variants, which are verified by hand; Level 3 gets only a paraphrased perturbed variant (pp. 5, 15-17). Levels 1-2 are scored by binary final-answer correctness (LLM-judged, +/-2%); Level 3 is scored by rubric, with LLM scoring and human calibration (pp. 6, 18-19). 16 LLMs were evaluated zero-shot (p. 6).
domain: engineering: three subfields, Systems & Control, Physical & Structural and Chemical & Biological, spanning electrical, mechanical, civil, chemical, aerospace and other disciplines (pp. 2, 5, 13)
size: 1,760 problems by its subfield counts (939 + 354 + 467), 43 of them Level 3 (p. 5); three variants per Level 1-2 problem and one per Level 3 problem (p. 5); 16 LLMs (p. 6)
source_of_items: perturbed from existing sets. Levels 1-2 come from public benchmarks, competition datasets and university assignments and exams, filtered and classified with LLM prompts plus human verification (pp. 5, 13-14). Level 3 comes from modelling competitions (CUMCM, MCM/ICM, APMCM, 2010-2024), translated and paraphrased by an LLM under expert supervision (pp. 14-15).
has_gold_traces: no: reference answers for Levels 1-2 (the released fields, pp. 17-18) and reference solutions from top-ranked competitors for Level 3 (p. 5); no gold intermediate steps are released or scored
evaluation: Levels 1-2: binary final-answer correctness against the reference, judged independently by GPT-4.1 and Gemini 2.5 Flash with +/-2% numerical tolerance, with disagreements resolved by hand. The judge prompt also asks the judge to check the core calculation steps, but it outputs only True or False (pp. 6, 18). Level 3: rubric scores (0-10) on four capability dimensions (information extraction, domain-specific reasoning, multi-objective decision-making, uncertainty handling), from GPT-4.1 and Gemini 2.5 Flash averaged, then reviewed and calibrated by human annotators (pp. 6, 18-19). Not step-level
human_validation: Level 3 problems and rubrics were reviewed by 20 PhD students and engineering professionals (p. 5). Each rubric was cross-checked by two reviewers with engineering backgrounds, and disagreements were settled by prize-winning modelling experts (p. 19). Level 1-2 variants were verified by hand (p. 15). The Level 1-2 judges were checked on 300 problems by hand: GPT-4.1 was 98.67% accurate and Gemini 2.5 Flash 98.33% (p. 18). At Level 3, LLM-only, human-calibrated and human-only scores are close and rank models similarly (Table 2, pp. 23-24). No inter-rater agreement statistic is reported.
contamination_measures: perturbations: LLM-rewritten variants with changed numbers and wording, meant 'to reduce possible overlap with pretraining data' (p. 5), and a paraphrased Level 3 (p. 15). Average Level 2 accuracy falls from 66.6% to 61.6% under perturbation (p. 24). Most source items are public (pp. 5, 13-14), and the rewrites are fixed at construction, not regenerated per evaluation

engtrace_use.sentence: S-E2 (L190-198): '...while broader efforts like EngiBench (Zhou et al., 2025) rely on subjective rubric-based scoring.' S-I3c (L116-122): 'EngTrace addresses both gaps through integrative reasoning templates that, unlike existing benchmarks (e.g., Zhou et al., 2025; Mudur et al., 2025) that rely solely on outcome matching, demand holistic procedural reasoning'. S-E3 (L199-201): 'existing benchmarks remain limited to outcome matching'.
engtrace_use.explanation: Each sentence is half true, and the two contradict each other (citation map C6). S-E2: rubric scoring covers only Level 3, 43 of 1,760 problems (p. 5); Levels 1-2 are scored by binary answer correctness (pp. 6, 18). So the benchmark as a whole does not 'rely on' rubrics. 'Subjective' is not supported either. The rubrics come from official competition scoring standards, refined and adjudicated by experts (pp. 5, 18-19), and LLM-only, human-calibrated and human-only scores agree closely (Table 2, p. 24), although no inter-rater statistic is given. S-I3c and S-E3: 'solely on outcome matching' fits Levels 1-2 but not Level 3, whose rubrics score assumptions, trade-off modelling and uncertainty handling (Figure 5b, p. 8; pp. 18-19). That is the protocol's own example of misleading: an outcome-only label on a benchmark that also scores more than the outcome. Both sentences also omit what matters most for EngTrace. EngiBench is the broadest engineering benchmark cited, with graded difficulty levels and a perturbation test against memorisation (pp. 5, 7). But it has no gold intermediate steps and no step-level scoring, and that, not rubric versus answer matching, is the real difference.

suggested_wording: EngiBench (Zhou et al., 2025) spans three engineering subfields at three levels. Its closed-form Levels 1 and 2, drawn from existing benchmarks and university materials and rewritten into perturbed, knowledge-enhanced and math-abstraction variants, are scored by final-answer correctness. Its 43 open-ended Level 3 modelling problems are scored by LLM judges, with human calibration, against expert-refined competition rubrics. No level checks intermediate steps against a gold trace.
facts_to_cite: Three levels: foundational knowledge retrieval, contextual reasoning, open-ended modelling (pp. 1, 4)

Levels 1-2 are closed-form problems drawn from existing benchmarks (e.g. SuperGPQA, MMLU, MATH, GSM8k, Omni-MATH, Big-Math) and university materials, kept by an engineering-relevance filter (pp. 5, 13-14)
Level 3: 43 open-ended problems from modelling competitions (CUMCM, MCM/ICM, APMCM, 2010-2024), kept from nearly 1,000 because they have official rubrics (pp. 5, 14-15)
1,760 problems across Systems & Control (939), Physical & Structural (354) and Chemical & Biological (467) (p. 5)
Each Level 1-2 problem has LLM-generated, hand-verified perturbed, knowledge-enhanced and math-abstraction variants; Level 3 has only a perturbed paraphrase (pp. 5, 15-17)
Levels 1-2 are scored by binary answer correctness, judged by GPT-4.1 and Gemini 2.5 Flash with +/-2% tolerance; on 300 problems checked by hand the judges were 98.67% and 98.33% accurate (pp. 6, 18)
Level 3 is scored on four capability dimensions by rubrics derived from official criteria and refined by experts, applied by two LLMs and calibrated by human annotators (pp. 6, 18-19)
16 LLMs evaluated zero-shot; all stay well below the human expert score of 8.74 on Level 3 (pp. 6-7)

Under perturbation, average Level 2 accuracy falls from 66.6% to 61.6% (p. 24); math-abstraction variants raise accuracy, which the authors take to mean that turning text into a mathematical formulation is the main difficulty (pp. 7-8)
overlap_with_engtrace: Shares: multi-branch engineering scope (chemical, mechanical, civil, electrical); graded difficulty; a perturbation test aimed at memorisation, close in purpose to EngTrace's paraphrase arm; LLM answer judges checked by human spot checks. Lacks: template-generated instances (most items are public problems with one fixed LLM rewrite each); gold intermediate traces; step-level evaluation; a private pool. EngTrace's answer check is deterministic, while EngiBench's is LLM-judged with a +/-2% tolerance (p. 18). Its Level 3 open-ended modelling has no counterpart in EngTrace.
notes: Naming clash: Felten et al. (2025) published a different 'EngiBench', an ML design-optimisation library (reviewed as felten2025engibench). The May bibliography note mentions it but gives it no entry. The text reviewed is v2 (2 May 2026); the May paper cited abs/2509.17677, probably v1 (Sept 2025), so some details (the human calibration, the 300-problem spot check, Table 2) may postdate the version the May authors read. Per the citation map's arXiv record, the author list (p. 1) shares Xiyuan Zhou, Yuheng Cheng, Huan Zhao, Wenxuan Liu, Yan Xu and Junhua Zhao with ElecBench, which S-E1 cites as 'Cheng et al., 2024'. EngiBench's own related work (p. 3) describes general-purpose benchmarks as emphasising 'factual recall in multiple-choice form' and classifies FEABench as task-oriented.
